newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech ministers rule out crown devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Czech ministers rule out crown devaluation.

text.p: A meeting of key members in the Czech cabinet dealing with country's trade and macroeconmic situation agreed on Tuesday that a devaluation of the crown was not a possible answer to solving a ballooning trade deficit, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said.
"A (devaluation) is not among the factors which we think could change something," Klaus told reporters after the meeting.

"We don't see the causes (of the deficit) in the level of the exchange rate, and therefore, none of the participants in the meeting proposed a change of the rate of the crown in any direction," Klaus added.

Last month, Klaus called the meeting of key economic ministers along with central bank governor Josef Tosovsky after the January-August trade deficit grew to more than 100 billion crowns, about the same as for the whole of 1995.
Analysts forecast the trade gap might push the current account deficit to over six percent of gross domestic product from four percent last year.
Klaus said the key thing to help exports was to have "consistent budgetary and monetary policies".
He added that there should be a clear signal from the government that rises in wages should follow increases in productivity, although he did not suggest any sort of new regulation to achieve that.
Klaus said the government would consider legislative changes to help build confidence in the banks and the capital markets.
"For trust in the Czech crown we need a quality banking system and capital markets," Klaus said, but declined to specify what new legislation was planned.

He repeated that he did not expect a reversal in the trend toward a worsening trade deficit, which the government has said is a necessary by-product of a growing and transforming economy, before the end of 1997.
Klaus said the government hoped to first slow the pace of the expansion of the deficit and then decrease the deficit.
"There is not reason to panic," he said.
Analysts have widely asserted that the current account deficit is capable of being financed by capital inflows, services, and tourism, at least in the short to medium term.
